title: Weights
body:
The learned parameters of a model: **the only thing training changes.** Everything else about a
[[Neural Network]] (how many layers, which [[Activation Function]], the learning rate) is chosen by
you before training starts and is fixed while it runs. The weights are what
[[Gradient Descent]] moves.

In a single [[Neuron]] a weight is one coefficient $w_i$, saying how much input $i$ counts toward
that unit's vote. Across a layer they stack into a [[Matrix]]: row $j$ of $W$ is the weight vector
of unit $j$, so the whole layer is one [[Matrix Multiplication]], which is what [[Forward Pass]]
means. Layer $\ell$ mapping $m$ inputs to $n$ units carries an $n \times m$ weight matrix plus $n$
[[Bias Term|biases]], and the model's parameter count is the sum of that over every layer.

## Why they are the thing that gets differentiated

Training asks one question per weight: **if I nudge $w$, does the [[Loss Function]] go up or down,
and how fast?** That is $\partial L / \partial w$, and the answer for every weight at once is what
[[Back Propagation]] computes. The update is then

$$
w \leftarrow w - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}
$$

with $\eta$ the learning rate. Nothing about that step is specific to networks; it is
[[Optimization]] from [[CALCULUS 1]] with too many variables for a closed form. See
[[Gradient Descent]].

## Initialisation is not a detail

Weights start at small random values, and both words matter:

- **Random**, because if every weight in a layer starts equal, every unit in that layer computes
  the same thing and receives the same gradient, so they stay identical forever. The layer has one
  unit's worth of capacity no matter how wide it is. This is the symmetry-breaking argument.
- **Small**, because large weights push [[Sigmoid|sigmoid]] units into their flat regions where the
  derivative is near zero and no gradient flows back.

Note that [[Bias Term|biases]] can safely start at zero: the random weights have already broken the
symmetry.

## The word means something else in COMP 2631

A [[Weighted Graph]]'s edge weights are given data, part of the problem statement, and algorithms
like [[Minimum Spanning Tree]] read them and never write them. These weights are unknowns being
solved for. Same word, opposite role.
